newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan warns against escalating tensions on Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: Annan warns against escalating tensions on Cyprus.

text.p: Secretary-General Kofi Annan joined a chorus of international concern on Friday over escalating tensions on the divided island of Cyprus and called for maximum restraint.

In his first such statement since taking office on Jan. 1, the new U.N. chief also reminded all sides the U.N. Charter forbade the threat or use of force. He stressed the importance of "carefully prepared face-to-face talks" between the leaders of the Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot communities.

The statement, issued through Annan's spokesman, Fred Eckhard, was prompted by a recently-concluded deal by the Greek Cypriot-led government in Nicosia to acquire Russian-made S-300 ground-to-air missiles, and by warnings by Turkey that it might launch an attack if they were deployed.
"The secretary-general is concerned by the increase in tensions on Cyprus," the statement said.

"The Security Council, most recently in its resolution 1092 of December 23 of last year, has expressed grave concern about the excessive levels of military forces and armaments in the Republic of Cyprus and the rate at which they are being expanded, upgraded and modernised, including the introduction of sophisticated weaponry.

"The secretary-general believes that the events of the past week once again underline the inherent instability of the status quo and add urgency to the concerted efforts to achieve an overall political settlement through negotiations."

The secretary-general "underscores the importance of carefully prepared face-to-face talks between the leaders," the statement said, referring to Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides, as head of the Greek Cypriot community, and Rauf Denktash, the Turkish Cypriot leader.

"He calls upon the parties to avoid risk of confrontation on the island and urges all parties to exercise maximum restraint. The secretary-general reminds all sides that the United Nations Charter forbids the threat or use of force in situations such as this," the statement concluded.
Cyprus has been virtually partitioned since 1974 when troops from Turkey took over the north of the island after a coup in Nicosia engineered by the junta then ruling Greece.
According to the United Nations, which has had a peace-keeping force on the island since 1964, more than 30,000 Turkish troops remain in northern Cyprus.
The internationally-recognised Cypriot government, whose National Guard numbers about 11,500, has a defence pact with Greece and has embarked on an arms-purchasing programme.

The acquisition of S-300 air-defence missiles with a 90-mile (145 km) range, though not expected to be deployed for a year or more, would deny Turkey air superiority over the island, which is only about 40 miles (65 kms) away.
The United States, Britain and France have all expressed concern over the missile deal, fearing it would not only fuel tensions in Cyprus but between NATO allies Greece and Turkey.

After Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller said "We will do what is needed" if the missiles were deployed, U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said this was "no time for the Turkish government to be making wild and dramatic statements which will not be supported by any sensible member of the international community."
Denktash also said on Friday if the missile plan were not scrapped, the abandoned Cypriot "ghost resort" of Varosha would be integrated into the Turkish sector of the island.
The United Nations has been trying unsuccessfully for decades to reunite Cyprus as a bizonal, bicommunal federation.

Preparations are already under way to launch a new diplomatic drive to resolve the long-festering problem. This has received added impetus because talks are expected to get under way early next year on a request by Cyprus for membership in the European Union.
The talks would be greatly complicated if the island were still divided.

The Turkish Cypriots proclaimed their own Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus in 1983, with Denktash as president. But it is recognised only by Ankara. They have said links with Turkey would be strengthened even further if the Nicosia government joined the EU while the island remained split.
